blocks.text: Halogenoalkanes are very useful in daily life, largely because of their chemical stability. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were once used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants, though they are being replaced by eco-friendly alternatives. In medicine, halogenated compounds are powerful anaesthetics, and halogenoalkanes are important intermediates in making polymers such as PVC (polyvinyl chloride) for pipes and PTFE (Teflon) for non-stick cookware.

Halothane, CF3-CHClBr, is a halogenated hydrocarbon widely used as a powerful inhaled anaesthetic: it causes a reversible loss of consciousness during surgery. Chloroform and other chlorinated anaesthetics used earlier are no longer used because of their toxicity.

blocks.alt: Displayed structure of halothane: a carbon with three F atoms (left, above, below) bonded to a second carbon that carries Cl above, H below and Br on the right.
blocks.caption: Structure of halothane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 76).

blocks.title: Halogenoalkane
blocks.text: A halogenoalkane forms when one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms (X = F, Cl, Br or I). With one, two, three or more halogen atoms it is a mono-, di-, tri- or polyhalogenoalkane. Monohalogenoalkanes are also called alkyl halides, R-X.

blocks.alt: Three displayed structures, each a carbon with H on the left and X on the right: monohalogenoalkane (H above and below), dihalogenoalkane (X above, H below) and trihalogenoalkane (X above and below).
blocks.caption: Mono-, di- and trihalogenoalkanes (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 76).

items: Primary: the carbon carrying X is joined to one or no other carbon atom, e.g. chloromethane CH3Cl, chloroethane CH3CH2Cl, 1-chloropropane CH3CH2CH2Cl.

blocks.alt: Three primary halogenoalkanes in boxes: CH3-Cl chloromethane, CH3-CH2-Cl chloroethane and CH3-CH2-CH2-Cl 1-chloropropane.
blocks.caption: Examples of primary halogenoalkanes (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 76).

items: Secondary: the carbon carrying X is joined to two other carbon atoms, e.g. 2-chloropropane (CH3)2CHCl and 2-chlorobutane CH3CHClCH2CH3.

blocks.alt: 2-chloropropane drawn as two CH3 groups joined to CH-Cl, and 2-chlorobutane, CH3-CH(Cl)-CH2-CH3, with the Cl above the second carbon.
blocks.caption: Examples of secondary halogenoalkanes (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 76).

items: Tertiary: the carbon carrying X is joined to three other carbon atoms, e.g. 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (CH3)3CCl.

blocks.alt: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane: a central carbon bonded to Cl on the right, H3C on the left and CH3 above and below.
blocks.caption: Example of a tertiary halogenoalkane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 76).
